entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Students spend two lessons each week deepening their understanding of the parts of speech. During the other two lessons, students grow their writing skills with composition assignments from their books. Throughout the year, they explore literary concepts such as point of view and experiment with multiple forms of writing, including letters, descriptions, short accounts, and poetry.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Language Study: Grade 8

Grammar/Comp: Grade 8
These lessons, combined with the writing practice students continue to gain through written narrations, reinforce concepts and build fluency with various types of written forms.

NARRATION vs. COMPOSITION
As students begin to have more formal composition assignments in addition to written narrations, it's important to consider the difference between the two. Both narrations and compositions build students' skills in writing. The focus in narrations is on building written fluency by "telling back" the reading in written/typed form (and students are free to experiment with various ways to do this or not, as interested). The focus in composition assignments is to give them accountability and structure to practice specific skills in one or more types of writing. 

Sometimes this means that a composition prompt assigns a specific type of "telling back" (such as retelling a reading as a poem, which a student may or may not have already experimented with of their own accord in their narrations). Additionally, compositions move beyond narration and variations of "telling back" to assignments which ask students to direct their attention to specific ideas within or across their readings (such as comparing and contrasting characters or texts) and other types of reflection which they previously have mainly practiced discussing orally or briefly in writing after reading and narrating in their lessons. Finally, especially as students enter high school, composition assignments merge with grammar assignments to help students understand the writing process more globally and consider aspects of style, editing, revision, research, and the ethics of communication.

lessons.title: 20m Grammar/Comp: Grade 8 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
➜ NOTE TO STUDENTS
One purpose of composition lessons is to encourage you, the student, to dig deeper, reflect on your readings, explore the different ways words work, and learn how to ask good questions of yourself and your readings. Set your timer and use the whole time allotted for a composition assignment. If you finish an assignment with extra time, explore another perspective, ask further questions, or take a bit more time to see if any other thoughts come to mind. Alternatively, if you find yourself stuck, you may want to take a short break and come back later! Growth, not frustration, is the goal.

➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #1 - Summary/Reflection
Write a brief summary of a current event. 
OR
Tell of a time when your desire for society was met. How did that experience impact/affect you?

➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #2 - Letter
Write a letter to a family member, friend, or imaginary character about one of your favorite books so far this year. Tell them what you think the book is about, why you like it so far, and then send the letter if you like!
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER TIP
Make sure students are practicing typing skills and typing narrations and compositions regularly. 

There are two designated lessons each week to work on the Composition prompts. All prompts will be listed in those lessons, so students can choose which prompts to work on.

Nouns
⍞ Materials: Grammar Voyage
 
➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.11-17  

➜ PRACTICE
• Copy the diagram on p.15. Discuss the size and placement of the elements. 
• For each noun in purple on p.16, is it a person, place, or thing?
• Copy the types of nouns in purple from p.17 and come up with your own example for each type. Discuss compound nouns, too.
lessons.teacherNotes:
• DEFINITIONS
A marine chronometer is a clock that is accurate enough to be used to calculate longitude via celestial navigation.

★ TEACHER NOTE
There are also COMPOUND NOUNS that combine words. They are sometimes hyphenated: mother-in-law, schoolteacher, toothpaste.

★ TEACHER NOTE
In modern usage, they and them have been adopted as singular pronouns that can replace a singular noun. For example: In the dictation lesson, the student will choose words that are unfamiliar to "them" (instead of saying "her or him"). If your child doesn't know French, "they" can start learning it this year (instead of "he or she").

lessons.title: 20m Grammar/Comp: Grade 8 - Lesson 10
lessons.body:
Pronouns, Adjectives
⍞ Materials: Grammar Voyage
 
➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.22-27  

➜ DISCUSS
Why is it important to make sure that the pronoun's antecedent is clear? Why is it better to say "modify" instead of "describe" to explain what adjectives do? How do adjectives modify pronouns?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
Emphasize the word modify because it is much more accurate than the word describe. When the adjective happens, the noun goes poof. Example: LADDER and CORPORATE LADDER

• Find nouns, pronouns, and adjectives in the first paragraph of Moby Dick on p.29. [See Answer Key] Remember that articles are special adjectives! 
• Find all the nouns in the passage on p.30. [31 of them, excluding the infinitive "to ebb"] How many are plural?

This would make a good small-group activity for a classroom setting, letting students work together to find as many nouns, pronouns, and adjectives as they can. This presents the opportunity to discuss items they did not see or to discuss why an item they chose is none of the three.

lessons.body:
➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #1 - Editing
Reread your second narration draft from last week. What you did is called "revision," because you are revising content. The next thing to do is to edit. When we edit, we look for sentence structure, misplaced modifiers, subject-verb disagreement, wordiness, spelling, weak words, etc. Write a third draft to correct mistakes and make each word pack a punch. Compare with your first draft. Which is better? Why?

Remember: All good writers revise and edit their work. It's a good thing to improve your writing and to find and fix errors! Very few people write perfect sentences the first time they put their ideas on paper (or type them). 

➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #2 - Personification
Look back through the poems you have read this year to find some examples of personification. An author uses personification when s/he gives an inanimate object or abstract idea the qualities of a person. One example is Pauline Johnson's "The Song My Paddle Sings," which you may have read last week in your Poetry course.
With the remaining time, try writing a few sentences of your own using personification. See what the most outlandish comparison you can make is!
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER TIP
Some students may find it helpful to use external supports before writing, such as index cards that can be arranged and re-ordered. You can also encourage students to talk aloud as they write or use speech-to-text and then edit.

lessons.body:
➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #1 - Poetry - Found Verse

➜ INTRO
Have you ever heard of "found poetry"? Learn more with the article below.
∞ Article Link: Found Poetry

➜ WRITE
Poets have used historical texts like William Bradford's History of Plimoth Plantation, newspapers, novels, and more to create found poems. The act of rearranging words, pulling words from different places together, and thinking about key images in a text is essentially a way to think more deeply about what you have read. For this assignment, just pick one passage from one of your favorite books as your source text. Use Little Women/Sir Gibbie if there isn't another book that comes to mind.

• Decide your selected passage (keep it short - no more than 1-2 pages).
• Highlight words or phrases you particularly like and/or which seem particularly important to the passage.
• Type or write those words on a separate piece of paper and use them to write a poem.
• You may choose whether to limit yourself to ONLY words found in your text or whether you want to add some of your own words as well.

➜ ⬚ 15m COMPOSITION ASSIGNMENT #2 - Found Verse Construction
Continue with your found verse project today, either by hand or online, by taking the words and phrases you underlined or highlighted and putting them onto a separate piece of paper or a separate Google Doc. Play with the words to make your own found verse version of the passage you chose. Experiment with different line breaks and feel free to get rid of a phrase you had initially underlined or add a new one in. Read your work aloud to check if it flows logically and makes sense. Then read it to someone else and see what they think!

The rest of the lesson will be spent on brainstorming for your expository paragraphs. These are paragraphs that explain something. They are used for most formal essays and research papers. Think about a topic you would like to write about. What are three things you could discuss about that topic? Make a list and put them in a logical order.

Example: Dogs
--Types of dogs
--Benefits of owning a dog

terms.content:
· Grammar Voyage: What are the eight parts of speech? [noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, conjunction, preposition, interjection]


· Practice Voyage "Sentences 1-4" p.12-15: Label the parts of speech (Level One Analysis) on the top line under each sentence. Write a comment about something in the sentence that you find interesting. [Practice Voyage Answer Key]

· Grammar Voyage/Practice Voyage: In each of the following sentences, tell the part of speech for the word in brackets (noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, preposition, conjunction, or interjection).
1. The [ships] formed a row in front of the marina.
2. The captain [nailed] the doubloon on the mast.
3. [The] freighter pulled slowly to a stop.
4. A smokestack rose [high] above the top of the bridge.
5. The sailors ran quickly [up] the gangplank.
6. [Wow], the storm lasted all night.
7. They did not arrive, but we kept waiting [at] the dock.
8. [She] made the new captain a better chart.

Answers
1. noun
2. verb
3. adjective
4. adverb
5. preposition
6. interjection
7. preposition
8. pronoun


· Grammar Voyage/Practice Voyage: In the following sentences, is the bracketed word a subject, predicate, direct object, indirect object, or subject complement?
9. The people in this harbor are very [friendly].
10. John could see the new [marina] from his cabin porthole.
11. The captain gave [Susan] a pair of binoculars.
12. It was [he] who rang the ship's bell yesterday.
13. The cook gave [Roberto] a sack of hot rolls from the galley.

Answers:
9. subject complement
10. direct object
11. indirect object
12. subject complement
13. indirect object

· Grammar Voyage/Practice Voyage: Is the bracketed phrase prepositional, appositive, gerund, participial, or infinitive?
1. [To navigate accurately] is an important skill.
2. Robert Trotman, [the former captain,] was invited on board.
3. The seagull sailed [over the top] of the ship.
4. [Giving good advice] is a captain's prerogative.
5. [Fallen down completely,] the rusty freighter brought back memories.

Answers
1. infinitive
2. appositive
3. prepositional
4. gerund
5. participle

· Grammar Voyage/Practice Voyage: Is the bracketed part a phrase, an independent clause, or a dependent clause?
6. Rochelle brought the maps, and [we brought the compass.]
7. [Sailing away] was an easy thing for Maria.
8. [As the terns flew over the ship,] we watched intently.
Is the sentence declarative, imperative, interrogative, or exclamatory?
9. Which ship has the cargo you told me about?
10. The tugboat almost hit the pier at the corner of the dock!
11. Go to the marina and buy some fresh vegetables and bread.
12. The cold currents flow past the island to the north.

Answers
6. independent clause
7. phrase
8. dependent clause
9. interrogative
10. exclamatory
11. imperative
12. declarative
